name: Sharada Peeth, Neelum Valley
deity: Devi as Sharada (Saraswati), goddess of learning and speech, the Saraswati of Kashmir
period: Ancient temple and seat of learning, cited in the Nilamata Purana and by Kalhana; a ruin today
dynasty: Traditionally linked to the Karkota era (Lalitaditya Muktapida, 8th century); not firmly proven
style: Kashmiri temple architecture; a ruined stone shrine on a raised plinth
summary: Sharada Peeth in the Neelum Valley is the ancient seat of Sharada, the Saraswati of Kashmir, where tradition places Sati's right hand and which is tied by name to the Sharada script; it stands in ruins in Pakistan-administered Kashmir, out of reach of Indian pilgrims.

sections.history: In the line "Kashmireshu Saraswati" of the Ashtadasha Shakti Peetha stotram, the Mother of learning is named as the goddess of Kashmir, and Sharada Peeth in the Neelum Valley is held to be her seat. The Nilamata Purana is cited as the earliest text to speak of it, and the chronicler Kalhana mentions the shrine in the Rajatarangini. From about the sixth to the twelfth century it is remembered as a celebrated temple and centre of learning, and the Sharada script of Kashmir is bound to it in name and tradition. Some attribute the building to Lalitaditya Muktapida in the eighth century, though no firm evidence settles it. Aurel Stein visited in 1892. Kashmiri Pandits count it among their three holiest sites, with Martand and Amarnath, and today it is a ruin.
sections.architecture: What survives is a ruined stone temple on a raised plinth, on the slope above the river. A broad stone stair climbs to it from the west, and the entrance is a gateway with the double porch typical of Kashmiri architecture. Within a surrounding quadrangle stands a square sanctum with a west-facing door and plain stone columns, parts of which still rose to a considerable height when Stein recorded them. The 2005 earthquake and long neglect have since taken their toll. Measurements quoted in different accounts vary, and the original roof and inner details are only partly known.
sections.legends: Tradition holds that when the body of Sati was divided, her right hand fell in this valley, and the stotram names the seat as Kashmireshu Saraswati. Another memory is of the sage Shandilya, who is said to have performed penance at Sharada Vana beside the upper Kishenganga and to have been granted a vision of the goddess as Sharada; the shrine is placed where mountain streams meet. Tradition also says that Adi Shankara came here and received the goddess's blessing. Whatever the telling, the place has long stood for the Mother as the giver of knowledge, and for a Kashmir that honoured the learned.
sections.festivals: Kashmiri Pandits once made an annual pilgrimage here in the bright fortnight of Bhadrapada, though accounts name different days. Since 1947 pilgrims from India have been unable to reach the site. A Sharada Devi temple was opened at Teetwal in Kupwara district, near the Line of Control, on 22 March 2023, built by the Save Sharda Committee, and devotees now gather there to keep the goddess's memory. Confirm all dates and arrangements locally.
sections.experience: Sharada Peeth cannot at present be visited from India. It lies across the Line of Control in Pakistan-administered Kashmir, and Indian pilgrims have had no access since 1947. In 2023 the Indian government spoke of a corridor on the Kartarpur model, but none has opened, and the Teetwal crossing has been closed since 2019. Devotees therefore turn to the Sharada Devi temple at Teetwal, which keeps the goddess's memory for Kashmiri Pandits. For a visitor on the Pakistani side the ruin is a place of memory rather than of daily worship, and it deserves quiet and respect.

visit.timings: The ruin keeps no regular temple hours or daily worship, and access varies with the political situation, so check current official advisories. The Sharada Devi temple at Teetwal, on the Indian side, keeps its own hours; confirm locally.
visit.dressCode: Modest clothing with shoulders and knees covered is appropriate at this sacred site and at the Teetwal temple. In the Neelum Valley, dress conservatively and follow local custom.
visit.photography: No rules are published for the ruin; treat it as a sacred and protected heritage site and photograph respectfully. Near the Line of Control, including at Teetwal, security personnel may restrict photography, so ask before taking pictures.
visit.gettingThere: The ruins stand in the village of Sharda on the Neelum River in Pakistan-administered Azad Kashmir, approached by the Neelum Valley road, and entry conditions and permissions for visitors are not verified, so consult official travel advisories. The site cannot be visited from India: pilgrims have had no access since 1947, and the Teetwal crossing in Kupwara district has been closed since 2019. The Teetwal temple can be reached by road from Srinagar via Kupwara, subject to local permissions.
